items.title: When a post is published, Postiz treats a media path that is not a web address as a file on the...
items.summary:
When a post is published, Postiz treats a media path that is not a web address as a file on the server's disk, but it does not check that the file lies inside the upload directory. A registered user can store a crafted media path with a post, get it past the checks that normally restrict it, and have the publishing worker read an arbitrary file and send it as an attachment to a Discord server the user controls.

The same unconfined reads can be reached through two further routes. One tells the caller whether a file exists and can exhaust the backend's memory, the other delivers the file the same way as the main route. Self-registration is open by default, so the attacker needs no existing account.

items.title: Postiz signs its session, invitation and password reset tokens with one shared secret and without...
items.summary:
Postiz signs its session, invitation and password reset tokens with one shared secret and without any marker of what a token is for. A route that refreshes the credentials of a browser-extension channel signed data taken from the request itself and stored the result where the requesting user can read it back. A user could therefore obtain a validly signed token containing any claims they choose, which the application accepts as a session, as an organization invitation with a chosen role, as a password reset or as an enterprise provisioning token.

A second, narrower route that creates team invitations signs extra fields from the request body in the same way.

items.title: Web::Simple versions before 0.035 for Perl allocate a buffer sized by the Content-Length header...
items.summary:
Web::Simple versions before 0.035 for Perl allocate a buffer sized by the Content-Length header for urlencoded body parameters.

Web::Dispatch::ParamParser::get_unpacked_body_from reads an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body using a single read call, with no cap and the return value ignored. Perl's read grows the buffer to the requested length before reading, so the declared Content-Length determines the allocation.

An attacker can trigger this through any route whose dispatch specification has a % body-parameter match, such as sub (POST + %name=), sending a Content-Length far larger than the body actually sent. No authentication is involved.

items.title: The aBlocks – Gutenberg Blocks, User Dashboard Builder, Popup Builder, Form Builder & Animation...
items.summary: The aBlocks – Gutenberg Blocks, User Dashboard Builder, Popup Builder, Form Builder & Animation Builder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 2.17.0 via the `/ablocks/v1/form-builder/registration` REST endpoint. The vulnerability exists because the endpoint is registered with `permission_callback => __return_true` and the `register()` handler reads `roleSlug` directly from attacker-controlled block attributes in `post_content` without ever verifying that the block's `formType` is `registration` — a condition that `RegistrationFormSanitizer::verify()` imposes only at save-time, meaning a Contributor can preserve an arbitrary `roleSlug` by saving a block with `formType='login'` and then triggering the endpoint via a valid `wp_rest` nonce and post-ownership check. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Contributor-level access and above, to escalate their WordPress role to Editor or any other non-administrator role and receive a fully authenticated session at the elevated privilege level via `WP_User::set_role()` and `wp_set_auth_cookie()`. Escalation is bounded below administrator-tier roles because `is_safe_registration_role()` rejects any role holding `manage_options`, `edit_users`, `delete_users`, `create_users`, `promote_users`, or `edit_theme_options`, meaning the highest practically reachable role on a standard WordPress installation is Editor.

items.title: Postiz lets a signed-in user ask the backend to run a function on one of their connected channels...
items.summary:
Postiz lets a signed-in user ask the backend to run a function on one of their connected channels. The backend did not restrict which functions can be requested, so a user could call internal helper functions that were never meant to be reachable from the web interface.

One of those helpers reads a file from the server's disk. A user who connects a channel whose stored token is a file path can have the backend return the contents of any file it can read, including its environment, which holds the secret used to sign login sessions, the database address and the credentials of connected services. Another helper makes the backend process exit with a single request. Self-registration is open by default, so no existing account and no action by another user is needed.

items.title: Craft CMS allows any authenticated control panel user to submit an element-search condition whose...
items.summary:
Craft CMS allows any authenticated control panel user to submit an element-search condition whose element selector is evaluated as a sandboxed Twig object template. Craft’s allowed column filter delegates property lookup to Yii ArrayHelper, outside Twig’s SecurityPolicy. Repeated single-segment lookups therefore bypass the sandbox’s empty property/method allowlists.



The vulnerable condition value is ultimately cast to an integer. That does not protect the secret: the template can return author ID 1 when a guessed key character is correct and an impossible ID otherwise. The JSON endpoint returns entries for the first case and an empty array for the second, forming a stable remote character oracle.



After recovering GeneralConfig::securityKey, the same user can compute Craft’s generic HMAC wire format offline. Signed parameters such as redirect are then accepted and passed to unsandboxed View::renderObjectTemplate(), where Twig’s string-callable form can invoke native PHP callables. The regression proof uses the harmless substr() callback and observes abcdef becoming cdef; it does not execute an OS command.

items.title: filelock: ReadWriteLock on the hard-link route deletes any directory another user renames onto its .filelock-* link directory name

That route is every connection on macOS since 4.1.1 and any POSIX process without a usable `/proc/self/fd` (a Linux path that names the process's own open files), such as a chroot or container that does not mount `/proc`.

Another local user who can rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can rename one of the directories of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the link directory's name, or onto a forged dead-holder name. Such a lock directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The lock user's process then deletes that tree and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and reports no error. Stock Linux with `/proc` mounted is not affected. items.title: filelock: ReadWriteLock on Windows acts on SQLite side files another local user places beside its database
items.summary:
On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.

With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. `I:N` (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. `A:L` (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that `Timeout` handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed.

items.title: filelock: On Windows an oplock on a soft lock's marker holds SoftFileLock.acquire() past its timeout and blocks the stale break
items.summary:
On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.

Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.

items.title: virtualenv: Temporary app-data can leave dangling seed package links
items.summary:
## Summary

The app-data seeder can leave an environment linked to temporary package files that virtualenv deletes when creation
finishes. The environment-variable and configuration-file forms of `symlink_app_data` can enable this state even though
the command-line flag is disabled for temporary app-data. The resulting environment depends on a cache pathname that its
owner no longer controls.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-ZOE2GEPC` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.
This draft records source review and functional remediation checks. The reporter's cross-account code-execution claim
has not been independently reproduced.

## Affected area

Integrity of app-data references after temporary cache cleanup.

## Attacker-controlled input

Symlink seeding must be enabled through `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA` or `symlink_app_data` in the configuration file,
and app-data setup must fall back to a temporary directory. A missing or unwritable configured cache can cause that
fallback. Ordinary copy seeding does not leave these references.

The security concern requires a shared temporary-directory parent where another account can acquire the deleted cache
pathname, followed by use of the affected environment. That account need not already be able to modify the environment
or the private cache while it exists. This differs from the security policy's excluded case of an account that already
controls live app-data contents. On a platform with a temporary-directory parent private to the environment owner, that
cross-account condition is absent. Windows functional checks do not establish cross-account exposure under Windows
defaults.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[symlink seeder](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/via_app_data/via_app_data.py),
[temporary cache cleanup](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/app_data/via_tempdir.py).

## Mechanism

When app-data setup falls back to a temporary directory, the command-line `--symlink-app-data` action is disabled. A
value supplied by `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA` or `virtualenv.ini` can still become the parser default, and the seeder
constructor accepts that value without rechecking the cache lifetime. It links `site-packages/pip` into the temporary
cache. Session cleanup deletes that cache, leaving a dangling link whose pathname can later be claimed by another
account on a shared temporary filesystem.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner ran its reproduction as two unprivileged users, with root used only to switch identities. The environment
owner had an unwritable home, so app-data fell back to `/tmp`. The control used the command-line flag and received a
real pip directory. With `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA=1`, the new environment instead contained a `pip` link into a
deleted `/tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX` directory. A second uid recreated the target path and placed a fake `pip/__init__.py` there.
When the owner ran `venv/bin/pip --version`, that module created a marker inside the owner's environment and printed
`this is not pip`.

The cross-account path requires a shared temporary parent, a second account able to claim the deleted name, and later
use of the environment. A private temporary parent removes that route. The report traces the incomplete temporary-cache
guard to #1661, first released in 20.0.6.
[Public fix PR #3437](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3437) copies packages whenever app-data is
temporary, whatever supplied the symlink option. The implementation review checked the remediation; it did not rerun the
cross-account reproduction.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Environment owner
    participant V as virtualenv seeder
    participant T as Temporary app-data in /tmp
    participant E as site-packages/pip link
    participant A as Other local acco

items.summary:
## Summary

The pip seeder acquires bundled wheels with download=False and lets pip access the index when --download is selected.
Index candidates on that path do not pass through virtualenv's wheel digest verification.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-74ALJBUF` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Wheel selection by the pip seeder when downloads are enabled.

## Attacker-controlled input

The pip seeder and download option must be selected. The finding concerns the default-index digest-verification policy.
Explicit custom-index settings already opt out of comparison against PyPI metadata; this patch retains that policy.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[pip seeder](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/pip_invoke.py).

## Mechanism

With `--seeder pip --download`, `PipInvoke.get_pip_install_cmd()` first calls `get_wheel(download=False)`, so
virtualenv's `download_wheel()` and `verify_wheel_digest()` are skipped. It then lets `pip install` consult the
configured index. An index wheel with the same package and version as the bundled wheel can be selected without
virtualenv comparing its SHA-256 with PyPI metadata. The default app-data seeder takes the verification path for the
same option.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner built a local index named in `pip.conf` that served a modified copy of the bundled pip wheel under the same
filename. In the control run, `virtualenv --download env-default` rejected the wheel with a digest mismatch. In the
second run, adding `--seeder pip` produced an environment whose installed `pip/__init__.py` matched the index wheel;

`BUG`.

`PIP_INDEX_URL`, `PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL`, and `PIP_INDEX` unset, so virtualenv's default-seeder PyPI comparison remained
active. This does not establish index control in the default PyPI setup. The unchecked pip-seeder download path is
older, while the comparison with the default seeder arose when digest verification was added in 21.7.12.
[PR #3430](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3430) acquires and verifies selected wheels before invoking pip with
index lookup disabled.

## Affected area

Xonsh reads a UTF-8 activation script using a legacy multibyte encoding such as GBK. Printable non-ASCII bytes can
change how the reader recognizes an adjacent quote. The report concerns POSIX activation. It does not establish exposure
through unrelated activators.

## Attacker-controlled input

The attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generated
activation script.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[xonsh quote()](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/xonsh/__init__.py),

in the file and backslash-escapes an embedded quote. Xonsh's `source` reads the file using `$XONSH_ENCODING`. With GBK
or Big5, the UTF-8 bytes of `中` end in `0xad`, which pairs with the following `0x5c` backslash as one decoded character.

items.summary:
## Summary

The app-data copy seeder uses shutil.copy, which preserves cached file modes independently of the current umask. A cache
populated under permissive permissions can therefore produce files with wider access in later environments.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-487MH6OW` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Permissions of files copied from app-data into a new environment.

## Attacker-controlled input

The cache must contain files created with broader permissions than the current environment creator intends. Another
account must also be able to traverse the new environment and reach those files. A private parent directory prevents
that access. No control of a private live cache is assumed.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[copy helpers](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/util/path/_sync.py).

## Mechanism

The default app-data seeder extracts a wheel into a reusable cache and copies its files into later environments with
`shutil.copy()`. That function applies the cached source mode to each destination file after creating it, overriding the
current run's umask. If the cache image was built under umask `000`, a later environment created under umask `022` can
receive mode-`0666` pip files. The cache may be private while the new environment is reachable by other local accounts.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner created two histories with separate private app-data caches. In the control, the owner's first run used
umask `022`; a later environment had no files writable by another account, and that account could not append to
`pip/__init__.py`. In the attack history, the first run used umask `000` and the later run still used `022`. The report
counted 478 of 493 environment files writable by others. A second unprivileged uid appended a line to pip, and
`bin/pip --version` ran it as the environment owner. The cache itself remained under a mode-`0700` home in both
histories.

An attacker cannot force the owner's earlier umask through this finding; the attack also needs a traversable
destination. A mode-`002` cache can expose group write access under suitable group permissions. The scanner dates
app-data copy seeding to #1578, first released in 20.0.2. [PR #3425](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3425)
creates copied files under a fixed non-writable-by-others policy further restricted by the current umask.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Environment owner
    participant C as Private app-data cache
    participant E as Later environment
    participant A as Other local account
    U->>C: first seed extraction under umask 000
    C-->>U: cached pip files have mode 0666
    U->>E: create environment under umask 022
    C->>E: shutil.copy reapplies mode 0666
    A->>E: append code to pip/__init__.py
    U->>E: run bin/pip --version
    E-->>U: appended code runs as owner
```

items.summary:
## Summary

Caller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the bash activation prompt. An attacker must influence the
value passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment and draw the prompt.

## Affected area

Bash runs with compatibility level 4.2 and draws the environment prompt. Its replacement-string behavior differs from
newer compatibility modes, leaving prompt text subject to a second interpretation. The report concerns POSIX activation.
It does not establish exposure through unrelated activators.

## Attacker-controlled input

The attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generated
activation script.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[bash prompt assembly](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh).

## Mechanism

`bin/activate` copies the prompt into `PS1`. A shell expands `PS1` again when it draws a prompt, so the value must
survive both the assignment and that later expansion. The bash and zsh branches escape for their usual prompt rules.
Three other paths still interpret prompt data as commands: dash sourcing `activate` directly, a child dash inheriting an
exported `PS1` from bash, and bash running at compatibility level 4.2 or lower. A value such as `x$(touch MARKER)y` then
runs `touch` on prompt display. Creating the environment does not run the payload.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's child-shell reproducer creates an environment with `--prompt 'x$(touch MARKER)y'`, sources `bin/activate`
in interactive bash, and starts interactive `sh` (dash). Its control leaves `PS1` unexported: neither shell creates
`MARKER`. With `PS1` exported, bash displays the prompt without executing the value, but the child dash creates
`MARKER`; the reproducer ends in `BUG`. The report gives separate console reproductions for direct dash activation and
bash compatibility level 4.2. The child-shell path can arise after another environment's activation has exported `PS1`.

The scanner linked this finding to [#3326](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3326) and its follow-up #3390. Those
changes cover the usual bash path but leave the three paths above. The proposed change in
[#3418](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3418) keeps a variable reference in `PS1`, so prompt text is expanded as
data when drawn. The private report's reproducer was run by the scanner; the later command-execution result was supplied
by the maintainer review. This advisory does not claim that every POSIX shell or every bash mode is affected.

## Introduced

The report traces direct dash sourcing to the first 20.x activator (20.0.0b1), and inherited `PS1` to #3390 (first
released in 21.14.7). It demonstrates the compatibility-level case on bash 5.2. Those historical boundaries come from
the report; the release confirmed by the maintainer is 21.14.8.

    participant B as Interactive bash
    participant D as Child dash

    V->>B: generated bin/activate
    B->>B: assign escaped prompt to PS1
    alt PS1 is not exported
        B->>D: start sh with its own PS1
        D-->>B: marker absent
    else PS1 is exported
        B->>D: start sh with inherited PS1
        D->>D: expand $(touch MARKER) on prompt draw
        D-->>B: marker created
    end

items.summary:
## Summary

The venv creator reads the standard library's generated pyvenv.cfg with splitlines() and merges all resulting keys over
virtualenv's configuration. Line-boundary characters from destination data can therefore become configuration structure
before output sanitization.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-6ZQHJ6VI` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Configuration readback by the stdlib venv creator.

## Attacker-controlled input

An untrusted caller must influence the destination pathname passed to the venv creator. That pathname must contain a
character that Python treats as a line boundary. The builtin creator follows a different configuration-writing path.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[venv readback](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/via_global_ref/venv.py),
[configuration parser](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/pyenv_cfg.py).

## Mechanism

With `--creator venv`, virtualenv asks the standard library to create an environment, reads its `pyvenv.cfg` with
`str.splitlines()`, and merges the parsed keys over virtualenv's chosen settings. CPython writes the destination into a
`command =` value without escaping every character that `splitlines()` recognizes as a line boundary. A destination
containing U+2028, for example, can therefore supply new `home` and `include-system-site-packages` keys during readback.
Virtualenv writes those keys as real configuration lines. The builtin creator does not use this readback path.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner used one destination value with U+2028 between `home = /attacker/chosen`,
`include-system-site-packages = true`, and an absorbing `x =` key. A `python -m venv --without-pip` control kept the
value inside its `command` line and reported the base interpreter's `sys._home`. `virtualenv --creator venv --no-seed`
on the same value wrote separate injected configuration lines and its interpreter reported
`sys._home = /attacker/chosen`. The path did not require a literal newline byte. The control establishes that the extra
keys came from virtualenv's readback, not from the standard library's initial file alone.

The altered `home` can change which standard-library files the interpreter loads if an attacker also controls that
location; `include-system-site-packages = true` weakens environment isolation. Choosing the venv creator is required,
either explicitly or through a rare fallback. The report traces the readback to the 20.x rewrite, first released in
20.0.0b1. [PR #3426](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3426) rejects line-boundary characters before creation and
rebuilds the final configuration from selected settings.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Destination supplier
    participant S as stdlib venv
    participant V as virtualenv readback
    participant C as Final pyvenv.cfg
    participant P as Environment Python
    A->>S: path contains U+2028 and home = /attacker/chosen
    S->>C: write path inside command value
    V->>C: read with splitlines()

## Summary

The venv creator reads the standard library's generated pyvenv.cfg with splitlines() and merges all resulting keys over
virtualenv's configuration. Line-boundary characters from destination data can therefore become configuration structure
before output sanitization.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-6ZQHJ6VI` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Configuration readback by the stdlib venv creator.

## Attacker-controlled input

An untrusted caller must influence the destination pathname passed to the venv creator. That pathname must contain a
character that Python treats as a line boundary. The builtin creator follows a different configuration-writing path.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[venv readback](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/via_global_ref/venv.py),
[configuration parser](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/pyenv_cfg.py).

## Mechanism

With `--creator venv`, virtualenv asks the standard library to create an environment, reads its `pyvenv.cfg` with
`str.splitlines()`, and merges the parsed keys over virtualenv's chosen settings. CPython writes the destination into a
`command =` value without escaping every character that `splitlines()` recognizes as a line boundary. A destination
containing U+2028, for example, can therefore supply new `home` and `include-system-site-packages` keys during readback.
Virtualenv writes those keys as real configuration lines. The builtin creator does not use this readback path.

value inside its `command` line and reported the base interpreter's `sys._home`. `virtualenv --creator venv --no-seed`
on the same value wrote separate injected configuration lines and its interpreter reported
`sys._home = /attacker/chosen`. The path did not require a literal newline byte. The control establishes that the extra
keys came from virtualenv's readback, not from the standard library's initial file alone.

The altered `home` can change which standard-library files the interpreter loads if an attacker also controls that
location; `include-system-site-packages = true` weakens environment isolation. Choosing the venv creator is required,
either explicitly or through a rare fallback. The report traces the readback to the 20.x rewrite, first released in
20.0.0b1. [PR #3426](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3426) rejects line-boundary characters before creation and
rebuilds the final configuration from selected settings.

items.title: virtualenv: Seed replacement does not contain metadata deletion paths
items.summary:
## Summary

The app-data seeder joins paths from existing distribution metadata to site-packages and deletes the resulting paths
without checking containment within the environment.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-SXOEHWP7` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Removal of a previously installed seed package.

## Attacker-controlled input

An environment being reused must contain distribution metadata influenced by another account. The invoking user must
have deletion rights over the paths named by that metadata. Installing a new environment without existing package
metadata does not enter this cleanup path.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[seed uninstall](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/via_app_data/pip_install/base.py).

## Mechanism

Before reinstalling a seed wheel, `PipInstall._uninstall_previous_version()` accepts an existing `pip-*.dist-info`
directory in the destination. `_uninstall_dist()` reads its `top_level.txt` and `RECORD`, joins each entry to
`site-packages`, and deletes the result. It does not check whether `..`, an absolute entry, or a linked parent takes the
path outside the environment. The default app-data seeder reaches this path when it reuses a tree containing
seed-package metadata; `--clear` removes that tree first.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner prepared a project with `.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/pip-1.0.dist-info/`. Its `top_level.txt`
contained `../../../../../Documents`; its `RECORD` named `../../../../../notes.txt,,`. The user's home initially held
`Documents/thesis/chapter1.txt` and `notes.txt`. Running `virtualenv .venv` exited successfully but removed both paths.
A control tree with `top_level.txt` set to `pip` and a normal `pip/__init__.py` RECORD entry left the home files in
place. The reproducer prints `BUG` only when the control files survive and both attack targets disappear.

The deletion uses the invoking user's permissions and runs during creation, before any use of the environment. It
requires an existing destination that another account could populate; a fresh empty environment does not supply hostile
metadata. The report traces this cleanup to #2186, first released in 20.8.1.
[PR #3428](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3428) checks each deletion path against the resolved environment root
and refuses to delete the root itself.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared .venv metadata
    participant V as App-data seeder
    participant P as site-packages
    participant H as User home
    A->>P: top_level.txt names ../../../../../Documents
    A->>P: RECORD names ../../../../../notes.txt
    V->>P: read pip-1.0.dist-info before reinstall
    P->>H: join entries without containment check
    V->>H: remove Documents and notes.txt
    V-->>A: virtualenv exits successfully
```

items.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` crashes the Node.js process when a malicious server returns a response with more than five content codings and closes the connection before sending the body. undici rejects such responses (a content-encoding limit), but it created the internal response stream before that check and returned without attaching an error listener or aborting the request. The early close then surfaces a content-length mismatch on that orphaned internal stream, which Node.js treats as an unhandled `error` and terminates the process. A remote, unauthenticated server can trigger this with a single response, even when the application correctly catches the `fetch()` rejection. undici 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. undici now validates the content-encoding chain before creating the internal body stream and aborts the response when the limit is exceeded, so no error can surface on an orphaned stream.

### Workarounds

None.

items.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `EventSource` client can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised Server-Sent Events peer. By sending millions of tiny completed `data:` fields with no blank event separator, or a single unfinished line split across many chunks, the parser retains a growing amount of per-field and per-chunk state. The byte-based `maxEventSize` and `maxResponseSize` limits do not bound that retained state, and `maxResponseSize` is enforced on the compressed body before decompression, so a small compressed response can expand into enough retained memory to terminate the process. The application only needs to maintain an `EventSource` connection to an untrusted peer, which controls only the response. Availability is the only impact.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which bound the retained EventSource parser state (the number of `data` fields and buffered chunks, the unfinished-line length, and per-field byte totals) independently of the byte limits.

### Workarounds

None.

items.title: undici vulnerable to Subresource Integrity bypass via non-lowercase algorithm tokens
items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` verifies Subresource Integrity (SRI) metadata by looking up the algorithm token in a lowercase-only set, but the SRI specification defines a valid token by its ASCII-lowercase form. A correct but non-lowercase token such as `SHA256-...` or `Sha256-...` is therefore treated as unknown and skipped. When no recognized algorithm remains, undici treats the integrity list as empty and accepts the response, so a server that returns a body different from the pinned digest passes the check.

An application that pins a response with a valid uppercase or mixed-case SRI token receives attacker-controlled bytes with no integrity error. The attacker needs only to control the response body, not the application's integrity metadata. The issue affects response integrity only. The regression was introduced in undici 7.15.0; releases 7.14.0 and earlier lowercase the token and are not affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `7.30.1` or `8.12.2`. undici now normalizes the algorithm token to ASCII lowercase before validating it and before selecting the strongest algorithm, so case variants of SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are verified correctly.

### Workarounds

Use lowercase algorithm tokens (`sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512`) in `integrity` metadata.

multer vulnerable to Denial of Service via a pending asynchronous fileFilter after request teardown
items.summary:
### Impact

When `multer` is configured with an asynchronous `fileFilter`, a single request can crash the Node.js process. If a request is aborted (for example when one file is rejected) while another file's async `fileFilter` is still pending, the pending callback later resumes a parsing stream that multer has already torn down. busboy then emits an error on a stream that no longer has an error listener, which Node raises as an unhandled `'error'` event, and the process exits. A single unauthenticated request is enough, so any application using `multer` with an asynchronous `fileFilter` is affected, regardless of storage engine. Uploads using a synchronous `fileFilter` are not affected.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `multer` `2.5.0` or later.

### Workarounds

Use a synchronous `fileFilter`.

items.title: LangGraph: Namespace labels containing `.` reach other namespaces in Postgres and SQLite stores
items.summary:
### Summary

The Postgres and SQLite stores save a namespace as its labels joined with `.`, so `("tenant", "bob")` and `("tenant.bob",)` map to the same stored namespace. `put` rejected labels containing `.`, but `get`, `search`, `delete`, `list_namespaces`, their async versions, and ops passed directly to `batch`/`abatch` did not. A caller that could pass such a label could read, overwrite or delete items in another namespace.

### Details

`BaseStore` checked namespace labels only in `put`/`aput`. The other methods passed the namespace on unchecked, and `batch`/`abatch` checked nothing, including the `PutOp` items inside them. `PostgresStore`, `AsyncPostgresStore`, `SqliteStore` and `AsyncSqliteStore` turn a namespace into text with `".".join(namespace)`, so a label containing `.` resolved to the namespace whose labels it spells out:

- `get(("tenant.bob",), key)`, `search(("tenant.bob",))` and `list_namespaces(prefix=("tenant.bob",))` returned data stored under `("tenant", "bob")`.
- `delete(("tenant.alice",), key)` deleted the item stored under `("tenant", "alice")`.
- `batch([PutOp(("tenant.bob",), key, value)])` overwrote the item stored under `("tenant", "bob")`.

All releases of `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres` before 3.1.3 and `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite` before 3.1.2 are affected. `InMemoryStore` compares namespaces as tuples and is not affected.

### Impact

You may be affected if you use one of these stores, rely on namespaces to keep users or tenants apart, and let untrusted input choose a namespace label that reaches a read, delete or `batch` call. Such input could read, overwrite or delete another tenant's items. Labels written through `put` could never contain `.`, so no stored data becomes unreachable after upgrading.

LangSmith Deployment: the HTTP store API already rejected such labels, but store calls made from graph code reached the same flaw. The Agent Server rejects these labels from versions 0.15.5 and 0.16.2. On LangSmith Cloud, new deployments and revisions already include the fix and existing deployments get it on their next revision; self-hosted deployments should upgrade.

### Remediation

Upgrade to `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres` 3.1.3 or `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite` 3.1.2. Both require `langgraph-checkpoint` 4.3.0, where `get`, `search`, `delete` and `list_namespaces` reject labels that are empty, are not strings, or contain `.` with `InvalidNamespaceError`, and the Postgres and SQLite stores apply the same check to every op passed to `batch`/`abatch`. Stores outside this repository that turn namespaces into delimited text can call `langgraph.store.base.validate_op_namespace` for each op they run.

items.title: Happy DOM: Incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33943: unsanitized import alias leads to host code execution
items.summary:
## Summary

The ESM compiler in `happy-dom@20.14.5` does not validate imported local binding aliases before interpolating them into generated JavaScript.

As a result, an invalid ESM import alias can be transformed into a valid JavaScript destructuring default initializer and executed.

This appears to be an alternate injection path and incomplete remediation of GHSA-6q6h-j7hj-3r64 / CVE-2026-33943. The previous fix validates `importName` in the local `export { ... }` handler, but the named import handler still places an unvalidated `alias` directly into code context.

These issues were confirmed through the public `Window` and `<script type="module">` APIs using the published `happy-dom` npm package. The PoC reaches the Node.js host `process`, obtains `node:fs`, and creates a proof directory on the host filesystem.

## Confirmed affected versions

The PoC was directly tested against:

- `happy-dom@17.0.0`
- `happy-dom@20.0.0`
- `happy-dom@20.1.0`
- `happy-dom@20.14.5`

The same PoC does not trigger on `happy-dom@16.8.1`.

The ESM compiler was introduced by commit `7bc831df2`, first released in `v17.0.0`. The vulnerable interpolation remains present through `v20.14.5`, the latest release at the time of testing.

Suggested affected range:

```text
>= 17.0.0, <= 20.14.5
```

No patched version is currently available.

## Preconditions

- JavaScript evaluation is enabled with `enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true`.
- Attacker-controlled HTML or module source is processed by Happy DOM.
- This may affect SSR, preview, scraping, or testing services that evaluate externally supplied HTML.

## Technical details

In `packages/happy-dom/src/module/ECMAScriptModuleCompiler.ts`, the named import handler splits an import specifier and extracts its alias:

```ts
const nameParts = part.trim().split(/\s+as\s+/);
const alias = (nameParts[1] || nameParts[0]).replace(/["']/g, '');
const name = nameParts[0].replace(/["']/g, '');

if (alias && name) {
  properties.push({ name, alias });
}
```

Unlike the patched `export { ... }` handler, the value of `alias` is not validated as a JavaScript identifier.

It is subsequently inserted directly into generated binding syntax:

```ts
newCodeStart += `let {${properties
  .map((property) =>
    property.alias
      ? `"${property.name}": ${property.alias}`
      : property.name
  )
  .join(', ')}} = $happy_dom.imports.get('${url}')${match[8]}`;
```

Consider the following source:

```js
import {
  missing as injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337
} from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };
```

This is invalid ECMAScript module syntax. Node.js rejects it at the `=` token.

Happy DOM instead transforms it into the equivalent of:

```js
let {
  "missing": injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337
} = $happy_dom.imports.get('https://poc.local/dep.json');
```

items.title: Wasmtime: Panic lowering a host-created component model stream into a guest that expects a different payload type
items.summary:
### Summary

Wasmtime may panic when the host lowers a component model `stream` or `future` into a guest, if the host created that stream or future with one payload type and the guest expects a different one. This can happen when an embedder creates a stream or future, passes it through a guest, receives it back under a type-erased type such as `StreamAny` or `FutureAny`, and then passes it to a guest function with a different payload type.

GHSA-63h4-6cx9-pjfj is a related advisory also fixing issues within this area, and this advisory is being issued for portions of Wasmtime that were not fixed as part of that advisory.

### Impact

This affects embedders that do all of the following:

1. Create streams or futures on the host with `StreamReader::new` or `FutureReader::new`
2. Pass them to guest code and receive them back as `StreamAny`, `FutureAny`, `Val::Stream`/`Val::Future`, or a typed reader whose payload is one of these.
3. Pass them on to a guest function whose `stream` or `future` payload type differs from the type the host created them with.

A guest can cause the mismatch in step 3 when it controls the types of the functions it exports or of the values it returns. In that case a malicious guest can make the host panic, a denial of service. Embedders that only use statically typed `StreamReader<T>`/`FutureReader<T>` with concrete payload types throughout, or that never pass streams or futures they created through a guest and back, are not affected.

items.title: Wasmtime: Bit-packing in Cranelift compiler causes silent overflow and miscompilation
items.summary:
## Summary

In Wasmtime prior to v43, the Cranelift compiler backend bit-packs its SSA value indices in a way that can result in silent overflow in release builds, and result in incorrect value references in the IR resulting in arbitrary miscompilation. A very large Wasm function body, or one that is specially crafted to use many SSA values, can use this to force type-confusion or other arbitrary side-effects and escape the sandbox.

Cranelift was changed in Wasmtime v43 to use a full `u32` index, with checks if that limit is exceeded, and so is no longer susceptible to this bug.

## Impact

A Wasmtime engine with default settings (using the Cranelift backend) on any architecture/platform could experience a sandbox escape from a specially-crafted Wasm module.

## Patches

Wasmtime v36.0.19 has been released which fixes this issue.

`SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` evict an unparsable marker (the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock) once a waiting contender has watched it unchanged for two seconds. `SoftFileLease` expires a lease the same way. The watch tells two looks apart by the marker's modification time (mtime) and inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alone.

Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), parks an empty file of its own at the lock path. It dates that file to a future tick of the kernel's coarse clock (a clock that advances in steps of 4 ms), lets the waiters of the user running the lock (the lock user below) watch it past two seconds, and unlinks it in that tick. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. items.title: Fallow: A `.*` glob segment let an analyzed repository make Fallow test paths in the parent of the project root
items.summary:
### Impact

Fallow expands some globs from the analyzed repository on disk. Before 3.34.0, a segment such as `.*`, `.?` or `..*` in such a glob also matched the special `..` entry. The `glob` crate tests `..` against a segment that starts with a literal `.`. Fallow validates plugin glob patterns and refuses absolute paths and `..` segments, but these segments passed that validation.

The attacker controls the repository content. The attacker must also be able to read the Fallow output, for example a CI log or a pull request comment. Then the attacker can learn if a file or directory exists in the parent of the project root:

- A plugin `fileExists` detection pattern such as `.*/marker.json` made the plugin active when `marker.json` existed in the parent directory.
- An external plugin `configPatterns` or `alwaysUsed` pattern could match a config file in the parent directory. When the plugin was active and declared `toolingDependencies`, the tooling detection credited the related dev dependency. An unused dependency finding could then disappear, and `--trace-dependency` printed the outside path.
- `fallow plugin-check` reported `path_exists: true` for a seeded entry that matched only in the parent directory.

Fallow tested only that these paths exist. It did not read or print the content of a file outside the project root through these globs.

The Jest, Vitest and Rstest project globs had the same `.*` problem, and the Jest and Vitest ones also read file content. GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5 describes that case.

### Patches

Fixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now rewrites a leading `.` in a wildcard segment to `[.]` before it expands the glob on disk. `[.]` matches the same hidden files and directories inside the project root. The `glob` crate does not test `..` against it.

### Workarounds

Run Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the `detection`, `configPatterns` and `alwaysUsed` patterns of its plugin files.

### Summary

A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's FlashPix (FPX) JPEG-tile decoder lets an attacker achieve arbitrary code execution by getting an application to open a single crafted file with `Image.open()`. The file is recognized by content (the OLE2 magic), not by extension, so any service that opens or thumbnails untrusted uploads with the optional `olefile` dependency installed is reachable with no user interaction. In the PoC below, opening one crafted file executes an attacker-chosen command on stock Pillow 12.2.0 (x86_64 Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39).

### Details

`FpxImagePlugin` decodes FlashPix (FPX) files, which are OLE2/CFBF compound documents.

`Image.open()` auto-detects them from the OLE2 magic `D0CF11E0...` whenever the optional `olefile` package is installed (Pillow's documented dependency for FPX/MIC support), regardless of the file's extension.

For a JPEG-compressed subimage (`compression == 2`), the plugin builds a `"jpeg"` decode tile and derives the `(rawmode, jpegmode)` pair from attacker-controlled FPX color IDs through the `MODES` table ([`src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py` L25-L32](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py#L25-L32)):

```python

    ...
    (0x00018000, 0x00017FFE): ("RGBA", "LA"),                # rawmode "LA"  (2 bytes/pixel)
    ...
    (0x00020000, 0x00020001, 0x00020002): ("RGB", "YCC;P"),  # rawmode "YCC;P"
}
```

The Imaging output buffer for the tile is sized for the rawmode (here `"LA"` = 2 bytes/pixel) ([`src/decode.c` L223-L226](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/decode.c#L223-L226)):

```c
state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;   // "LA" gives 2 * xsize bytes/row
...
state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes);
```

In `JpegDecode.c` the rawmode string is mapped to a libjpeg `out_color_space`. Recognized modes (`CMYK`, `YCbCr`, `YCbCrK`, and so on) get a concrete colorspace, but `"LA"` and `"YCC;P"` are not recognized, so control reaches the fallback branch ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L219-L221](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L219-L221)):

```c
/* Disable decoder conversions. */
context->cinfo.jpeg_color_space = JCS_UNKNOWN;
context->cinfo.out_color_space  = JCS_UNKNOWN;
```

Under `JCS_UNKNOWN`, libjpeg performs no color conversion and emits `cinfo.num_components` bytes per pixel, taken from the embedded JPEG's SOF marker, which the attacker sets to 4. So `jpeg_read_scanlines` writes `4 * width` bytes per row into a buffer allocated for only `2 * width` bytes ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L252](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L252)):

```c

items.title: postal-mime: Quadratic CPU consumption when decoding a header of many joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words
items.summary:
### Impact

Decoding a header that holds a long run of joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words, such as `=?utf-8?B?QUJD?=` repeated tens of thousands of times in a `Subject`, `From`, `To`, a filename or a description, took time quadratic in the number of words. The join check ran a regex over the text joined so far for every word, which flattens the accumulated string each time. A single well formed message of about 1.6 MB blocked the event loop for one to twenty seconds depending on the host, and inline `message/rfc822` parts multiplied the cost, since each nested message carried its own header budget.

Any application that parses untrusted mail with postal-mime 3.0.0 through 4.0.7, including the exported `decodeWords()` helper, is affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

### Patches

Fixed in 4.0.8. The pad check now tracks the last appended word instead of testing the joined text, so decoding is linear in the header length. The same release also counts the parts and header bytes of inline `message/rfc822` sub-messages against the limits of the message as a whole, counts every header line for at least 64 bytes of `maxHeadersSize`, and adds a scaling test that measures every stage of the parser at two input sizes.

### Workarounds

Lower `maxHeadersSize` from its 2 MiB default to bound the cost per message, or parse untrusted mail in a worker that can be terminated.

### Credits

Reported by Felipe Fernández.

items.title: Pillow: Arrow export leaks stale heap memory when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT > 1
items.summary:
### Summary

When [`PILLOW_ALIGNMENT`](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/block_allocator.html#memory-pools) is set above 1, exporting an image to Arrow returns uninitialized heap memory mixed in with the pixel data. That memory can include pixels from images the process freed earlier. 

### Details

With an alignment above 1, the default allocator pads each row up to `aligned_linesize` and starts the first row at an aligned offset into the block. It then exports `im->blocks[0].ptr` as `xsize * ysize` tightly packed pixels, so exported data includes the padding bytes, and can include a few bytes from before the first row.

Tested vulnerable on 11.2.1, 12.3.0, 4c1ed27a5.

### PoC

Whether things leak may depend on allocator configuration. This does show a leak on my Mac.

```python
import os

os.environ["PILLOW_ALIGNMENT"] = "64"

from PIL import Image

# Image A: 64 px wide, so its rows fill the whole aligned stride
a = Image.new("L", (64, 40), 0x41).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)
del a

# Image B: 61 px wide, so each row has 3 bytes of padding; its pixels are all 0
b = Image.new("L", (61, 40), 0).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)

try:
    exported = Image.fromarrow(b, b.mode, b.size).tobytes()
except ValueError as e:
    print("Not vulnerable:", e)
else:
    if leaked := len(exported) - exported.count(0):
        raise RuntimeError(f"{leaked} of {len(exported)} exported bytes are not B's pixels")
```

### Impact

Information disclosure for applications that set `PILLOW_ALIGNMENT` and export images to Arrow. Likely any image whose row length isn't a multiple of the alignment will do. In a service handling several users' images, one user's exported data can contain pixels from another user's image, or other stale heap contents.
